process_characterization_report_structur.section: Reference to CQAs and supporting risk assessments
process_characterization_report_structur.content: Cross-reference the Critical Quality Attributes and the criticality/quality risk assessments that drove the characterization scope (verbatim item 1 of the Process Design Report content list, PAGE 34; CQAs with criticality risk assessment are a Stage 1 deliverable, PAGE 20).
Block/flow diagram depicting each unit operation at a similar level of detail (PAGE 34; example TFF process diagram Figure 3.4-1, PAGE 23).

Per-unit-operation description tables giving process requirements/raw materials/scale/order, set points and ranges, material flows, testing/sampling/IPCs, hold times/conditions, estimated yields and durations, equipment sizing, and component identification (PAGE 34; content of a process description PAGE 22; example Table 3.4-1, PAGE 24).
The in-process controls that are inputs to each step (verbatim item, PAGE 34).

process_characterization_report_structur.section: Outputs (in-process tests and limits, in-process specifications)
process_characterization_report_structur.content: In-process tests, limits and in-process specifications that are process outputs (verbatim item, PAGE 34).
Set points and ranges (NORs and, where supported by data, PARs) for each process parameter (PAGE 34; NOR/PAR designation PAGE 33).

process_characterization_report_structur.section: Classification of parameters for risk of impact to CQAs and process performance
process_characterization_report_structur.content: Parameter designations (CPP / KPP / Non-KPP) assigned via the criticality decision tree and quality risk assessment (PAGE 34; decision tree Figure 3.6-1 PAGE 30; designation definitions PAGE 15).

The multidimensional combination/interaction of input variables and process parameters demonstrated to assure quality, when an enhanced/QbD approach with multivariate DoE is used (PAGE 34; Design Space definition PAGE 15; established via multivariate designed experiments PAGE 31).

process_characterization_report_structur.section: Justification and data supporting all parameter ranges
process_characterization_report_structur.content: Supporting evidence for every parameter range: characterization/robustness study data, development studies, and clinical manufacturing history; the report is the repository linking process description, risk assessments, control-strategy description, characterization reports, rationale for parameter designations, and clinical manufacturing history (PAGE 34; role as PPQ justification PAGE 40).

Stage 1 deliverable that predefines the set of documented studies in which parameters are purposely varied over proposed/wider ranges to determine effect on CQAs and process performance, including univariate PAR studies and multivariate DoE for interactions (deliverable list PAGE 20; definition of process characterization PAGE 31).
Individual characterization/robustness study data reports feeding the design report; used to define PPQ ranges and acceptance criteria (deliverable list PAGE 20; PAGE 31).

Verification and qualification of laboratory/scaled-down models used for characterization, confirming representativeness of full-scale (comparing operational parameters, inputs/outputs including product quality attributes) (PAGE 31; Scale-up/Scale-down evaluation deliverable PAGE 20).
Tests on DS/DP/critical intermediates not in the routine release panel that are needed to claim comprehensive product/process understanding (Section 3.8, PAGE 31-32; deliverable list PAGE 20).

Planned set of controls derived from the characterization understanding: raw material controls, in-process and release specifications, IPCs, performance parameters, parameter set points and ranges (NOR/PAR), process monitoring, processing/hold times, and PAT where used (Section 3.9, PAGE 32-33).

key_terms.definition: A planned set of controls, derived from current product and process understanding, that ensures process performance and product quality; can include parameters/attributes for DS and DP materials/components, facility and equipment operating conditions, in-process controls, finished product specifications, and associated methods and frequency of monitoring and control (PAGE 15).

The multidimensional combination and interaction of input variables (e.g., material attributes) and process parameters demonstrated to provide assurance of quality. Working within it is not a change; moving out is a change normally initiating a regulatory post-approval change; proposed by applicant, subject to regulatory approval (PAGE 15).

key_terms.term: Formal Experimental Design / Design of Experiments (DoE)
key_terms.definition: A structured, organized method for determining the relationship between factors affecting a process and the output of that process (PAGE 15).

A systematic approach to development that begins with predefined objectives and emphasizes product and process understanding and process control, based on sound science and quality risk management (PAGE 16).
A prospective summary of the quality characteristics of a drug product that ideally will be achieved to ensure the desired quality, taking into account safety and efficacy (PAGE 16).

Referenced throughout as inherent attributes providing desired activity, purity and safety; criticality is assigned via risk assessment (case study PAGE 83; identification of CQAs is a Stage 1 deliverable PAGE 20). Examples given: deamidation, aggregate, host cell protein, residual DNA (PAGE 83).
A process parameter whose variability has an impact on a critical quality attribute and therefore should be monitored or controlled to ensure the process produces the desired quality (PAGE 15).

An input process parameter that should be carefully controlled within a narrow range and is essential for process performance; does not affect product quality attributes. If the acceptable range is exceeded it may affect the process (e.g., yield, duration) but not product quality (PAGE 15).
An input parameter demonstrated to be easily controlled or having a wide acceptable limit; may impact quality or process performance only if acceptable limits are exceeded (PAGE 15).

An input variable or condition of the manufacturing process that can be directly controlled; typically physical or chemical (e.g., temperature, process time, column flow rate, column wash volume, reagent concentration, buffer pH) (PAGE 16).
A characterized range of a process parameter for which operation within this range, while keeping other parameters constant, results in producing material meeting relevant quality criteria (PAGE 16).

A defined range, within (or equal to) the PAR, specified in the manufacturing instructions as the target and range at which a process parameter is controlled while producing material meeting release criteria and CQAs (PAGE 15).
Ability of a process to tolerate variability of materials and changes of the process and equipment without negative impact on quality (PAGE 16).

A system for designing, analyzing, and controlling manufacturing through timely measurements (during processing) of critical quality and performance attributes of raw and in-process materials and processes, with the goal of ensuring final product quality (PAGE 16).

A set of conditions encompassing upper and lower processing limits and circumstances (including within SOPs) that pose the greatest chance of process or product failure vs ideal conditions; such conditions do not necessarily induce failure (PAGE 17).

Development of a production strategy for a new drug starting from manufacturing processes similar to those used for other drugs of the same type, for which considerable experience already exists (PAGE 16).

An enabling system applied throughout the lifecycle; risk assessment should occur early, be controlled and effectively communicated, increasing product/process knowledge and lowering residual risk to patients (Section 6.1, PAGE 59).

doe_and_statistics_guidance: TR 60 (Section 6.2.1, PAGE 65-66) frames DoE as a core Stage-1 Process Design tool (Table 6.2-1 marks DoE, Measurement Systems Analysis/Gauge R&R, Robust Process Design/Tolerance Analysis/Taguchi, Multi-Vari Chart, and Regression/Correlation as Stage-1 tools; Descriptive statistics, SPC charts, Statistical Power/Sample Size, Process Capability, ANOVA, Levene/Brown-Forsyth/Bartlett/Fmax, Hypothesis tests/Confidence intervals span all stages) (PAGE 63-64). Goals of DoE: determine which input parameters significantly affect output CQAs; help determine design-space levels; optimize outputs (yield, impurity levels); and find input levels giving a robust process insensitive to parameter variability. DoE is contrasted with the classical one-factor-at-a-time approach, which cannot detect interactions. Recommended workflow: (1) Identify input parameters and output quality attributes as a team; for many parameters use a screening design such as a fractional factorial or Plackett-Burman to find the critical few; for changes to an existing process, build a Multi-Vari chart or SPC chart from current data to locate the largest variance source (within-batch, between-batch, positional) and expose 'lurking variables'; ensure the process is in statistical control before experimentation. (2) Run experiments to determine main and interaction effects, usually a full 2-level factorial for two to four parameters (2^2=4, 2^3=8, 2^4=16 runs), rarely beyond four factors; use fractional factorials (one-half or one-quarter) for four to six parameters; include center/control runs at nominal midpoints, run at the beginning and end (ideally during) to detect process drift, estimate inherent experimental error via replicate center points, and check for curvature; determine parameter effects on both mean and variation to build a robust process (standard DoE or Taguchi method). (3) Optimize with response surface experiments (three to five levels) to build an equation modeling input-output relationships and define the design space; common designs are Box-Behnken, central composite, 3-level full factorial, and computer-generated D- and G-optimal designs; analyze via regression using Minitab, JMP, or SAS; use quadratic/interaction effects to place set points in 'forgiving' regions away from boundaries of rapid quality deterioration. Multivariate DoE is the element of process characterization used to define design space, while univariate studies are appropriate for establishing PARs for some variables (PAGE 31). Statistical methods are also recommended, where practical, to justify the number of PPQ batches/sampling plans (PAGE 43). Additional methods reference PDA TR 59 and Appendix 8.1.
risk_assessment_guidance: Risk assessment is the driver that focuses process characterization and builds the control strategy. Stage-1 flow: perform an initial quality risk assessment to give a risk-based categorization of parameters BEFORE characterization, then perform process characterization experiments to set the design space, then perform a second risk assessment to establish parameter criticality and the control strategy (PAGE 18-20). Process characterization uses knowledge from the risk assessments to select which studies, ranges, and interactions to examine (PAGE 31). A decision tree (Figure 3.6-1, PAGE 30) assigns each variable as a parameter or attribute (by direct controllability), then designates CPP (potential impact to CQAs), KPP (impact to process performance/consistency), or Non-KPP (low risk over a wide range); risk assessment scores Severity, Likelihood, and Detectability. The tree is used both before and after characterization data are available: a parameter initially classed CPP may be re-designated non-CPP if robustness studies show CQAs are not impacted despite exaggerated variation (the second risk assessment re-scores) (PAGE 29). Quality Risk Management is treated as an enabling system (Section 6.1): in Stage 1 it drives identification of quality-affecting product attributes, criticality analysis for CQA identification, Cause-and-Effect Analysis or Risk Ranking and Filtering to link process steps/parameters to performance or quality and screen variables for future characterization/DoE, and Preliminary Hazards Analysis or early FMEA; in the Stage 1-2 transition it determines process control strategies addressing risk of failure per step and evaluates residual risk after mitigation (PAGE 59-60). Risk-based approaches also balance the number of PPQ batches against process risk (PAGE 43). Case study: a modified FMEA (QRA) using a template from similar products gave the initial parameter categorization and the initial control-strategy framework based on high risks; characterization then required QRA re-scoring and control-strategy update (PAGE 83-84).
case_study_parameters: Example unit operation (Table 3.4-1, TFF step, PAGE 24-27): Membrane Area set point 2 m2; Molecular Wt Cut-Off 30 kDa; Membrane Polymer Polysulfone

Pre-use cleaning: Cleaning Solution 0.4 to 0.6 N NaOH (Non-Key); Recirculation rate SP 10 L/min, PAR 8 to 12 L/min (Non-Key); TMP SP 10 PSI, PAR 5 to 15 PSI (Non-Key); Temperature SP 30 C, PAR 25 to 35 C (Non-Key); Time SP 60 min, PAR 60 to 90 min (Non-Key); WFI Flush volume SP 20 L/m2, PAR >=20 L/m2 (Non-Key)
Pre-use qualification: Integrity Test Pressure SP 15 PSIG, PAR 15-18 PSIG (Critical); Water Flux TMP SP 10 PSIG, 8-12 PSIG (Non-Key); Water Flux Temperature SP 20 C, 18-22 C (Non-Key)

Initial concentration step: Initial Product Total Mass SP 1225 g, PAR 900 to 1600 g (Critical); Initial Product Volume SP 75 L, PAR 50 to 100 L (Key); Recirculation rate 8 L/min, 6 to 10 L/min (Key); TMP 12 PSI, 10 to 15 PSI (Key); Temperature 20 C, 15 to 25 C (Non-Key); Process Flux (average) 20 to 30 LMH (Process Performance Attribute); Product Concentration 30 to 40 g/L (CQA); Product/Retentate Volume SP 35 L, 30 to 40 L (Critical)

Diafiltration step (constant volume): System Volume 35 L, 30 to 40 L (Critical); Number of Diavolumes SP 7, PAR 7 to 10 (Critical); Process Flux (average) 25 to 30 LMH (Process Performance Attribute); Recirculation rate 8 L/min, 6 to 10 L/min (Key); TMP 12 PSI, 10 to 15 PSI (Key)

Final concentration & recovery: Recirculation rate 8 L/min, 6 to 10 L/min (Key); TMP 10 PSI, 5 to 15 PSI (Key); Temperature 20 C, 15 to 25 C (Non-Key); Process Flux (average) 15 to 20 LMH (Process Performance Attribute)

Large-molecule case study (humanized IgG1, Table 7.1-1, PAGE 83): unit operations = Seed train, bioreactor, harvest, Protein A, viral inactivation, column purification 2, column purification 3, viral filtration, UFDF
IgG1 QTPP: IV administration at fixed dosage; liquid formulation at 20 mg/mL, iso-osmolar; single-use vial; shelf life at least 24 months at 2-8 C
IgG1 CQAs (examples): Deamidation, Aggregate, Host Cell Protein, Residual DNA
IgG1 clinical manufacturing scale: First-in-Human and Phase 2 at 2000 L bioreactor; Phase 3 at a different 2000 L bioreactor facility; commercial site identified at 12K (12000 L) bioreactor capacity
IgG1 Upstream process parameters characterized: Viable cell density, % Viability, Temperature, pH, Dissolved Oxygen
IgG1 Downstream process parameters characterized: Protein load, Protein concentration, Elution buffer pH, Viral inactivation pH, Diafiltration volumes

IgG1 characterization approach: DoEs from screening designs to full factorial used to understand interactions of high-risk parameters and develop a design space where possible; scale-down models created/qualified (e.g., virus clearance); modified FMEA used for QRA
Small-molecule pilot-scale representativeness (Section 3.7, PAGE 31): for solid/liquid oral dosage forms, 10% of commercial batch size and/or 100,000 units considered a representative scale

Oral solid dosage support example (PAGE 42): at least 8 Stage 1 batches (clinical supply, stability, pilot, process evaluation/design, plant demonstration) with same commercial formulation used to justify number of PPQ batches; unit operations wet granulation, fluid-bed drying, milling, blending, compression, film coating
